sections.title: AIF-C01 Crash Course: AWS Certified AI Practitioner

keyTerms.definition: AWS Certified AI Practitioner; the exam this volume covers in one linear pass.
The compressed trees used to confirm knowledge after the first read.

recall.question: How should you use this volume?
recall.answer: Read it once in a linear pass, then use the decision trees and practice questions to confirm the knowledge.

keyTerms.definition: AWS Certified AI Practitioner: 65 questions, 90 minutes, 700 out of 1000 to pass.
Scoring where strength in one domain offsets weakness in another; no per-domain minimum.
15 of the 65 questions do not count, and you cannot tell which is which.

recall.question: What are the exam's four numbers?
recall.answer: 65 questions, 90 minutes, 700 out of 1000 to pass, and about 83 seconds per question, so keep moving.

recall.question: Where should study time go?
recall.answer: Domains 2 and 3: together they are 52% of the exam.

keyTerms.definition: The exit test for each study rung; a rung only counts if you do each one.
The three compressed trees: customization, inference, and the service map.

recall.question: What are the three study rungs and their exit tests?
recall.answer: 20 minutes: the exam summary plus the three decision trees. 3 hours: one domain at a time with knowledge checks. 1 day: all 20 practice questions, re-reading every section missed.

sections.title: D1 · Fundamentals of AI and ML (20%)

keyTerms.definition: Learning with an answer key: every training example carries its label.
Learning with no answer key: finds natural groups in unlabeled data.
An agent takes actions in an environment and learns from the rewards.
The model memorized the training data, noise included, so it fails on new data.
The using phase: the finished model makes predictions on new data.
One API serving many foundation models; no training and no servers to manage.

recall.question: Five years of labeled cancel-or-stay records predict churn. Which learning type?
recall.answer: Supervised learning: the records are labeled and the task predicts a category.

recall.question: A chatbot answers shoppers while 5 million loan applications score nightly. Which inference types?
recall.answer: The chatbot is real-time and interactive; the nightly bulk scoring is batch.

recall.question: Name the service from the verb: chatbot, search company documents, call recording to text.
recall.answer: Lex builds the chatbot, Kendra searches the documents, Transcribe converts the call recording.

keyTerms.definition: Chunks of text smaller than words; the unit the system counts and prices.
The model's working memory: the maximum tokens it can consider at once.
Text turned into lists of numbers where similar meanings sit near each other.
Attention inside one sentence: each word weighs every other word's relevance.
Image generators that start from noise and remove it step by step, guided by text.
The open standard for connecting agents to external systems and data.

recall.question: A request uses 2,000 input tokens at $3 per million and 500 output tokens at $15 per million. What does it cost?
recall.answer: $0.006 for input plus $0.0075 for output, $0.0135 total; the smaller output half costs more than the input half.

recall.question: Documents were embedded with model X, then queries switched to cheaper model Y, and retrieval collapsed. What broke?
recall.answer: Each embedding model has its own private vector space, so ingest and query must use the same model.

recall.question: What distinguishes an agent from a chatbot?
recall.answer: A chatbot answers questions; an agent takes actions through tools in a reason, act, observe loop.

keyTerms.definition: Rewriting the prompt to change behavior; costs nothing and adds no new knowledge.
Fetching facts at query time into the prompt; new knowledge without touching the weights.
Continuing training on labeled examples so new behavior lands in the weights.
The creativity knob from 0 to about 1; near 0 the output is focused and repeatable.
Asking the model to think step by step; best for math and multi-step logic.
The automatic metric measuring overlap with reference summaries.

recall.question: A 4,000-page manual changes weekly and answers must cite the page. Which approach fits?
recall.answer: RAG with Bedrock Knowledge Bases: weekly changes make fine-tuning go stale within days, and citations need retrieval.

recall.question: A support bot needs a warm, playful brand voice while facts rarely change. Which approach fits?
recall.answer: Fine-tune on example conversations: the need is behavior and tone, not facts.

recall.question: A model keeps getting multi-step word problems wrong. Which prompt technique helps most?
recall.answer: Chain-of-thought: asking the model to reason step by step before answering improves multi-step reasoning.

keyTerms.definition: The system treating some groups worse than others, learned from data and repeated at scale.
Data reflecting past discrimination, like old hiring records that favored one group.
Filters around the model: block toxicity, redact PII, refuse off-topic requests.
Finds bias in data and models and explains individual predictions.
Documents a model's intended use, training data, metrics, and limitations.
Amazon Augmented AI: routes low-confidence or sensitive predictions to human reviewers.

recall.question: A bank must prove its loan model does not discriminate by zip code. Which tool fits?
recall.answer: SageMaker Clarify: it detects bias with subgroup analysis.

recall.question: What is the difference between transparent and explainable?
recall.answer: Transparent means you can see how the system works; explainable means you can say why it made one specific decision.

recall.question: A chatbot must refuse to output personal phone numbers. Which tool fits?
recall.answer: Bedrock Guardrails: it filters PII out of outputs.

keyTerms.definition: AWS secures the cloud itself; you secure what you put in it.
Grant only the access a workload needs, nothing more.
Malicious instructions smuggled into the model's input.
Logs every API call with caller identity: the audit trail.
Checks resources against compliance rules and records configuration history.
Collects evidence for audits automatically.

recall.question: A company leaves its S3 bucket public and uses it to fine-tune a Bedrock model. Whose failure is that?
recall.answer: The customer's: AWS secures the S3 infrastructure, but access control on the bucket is the customer's job.

recall.question: An auditor wants every Bedrock API call from last quarter with caller and time. Which service?
recall.answer: CloudTrail: it logs every API call with caller identity and timestamp.

recall.question: Name the two Bedrock privacy facts the exam loves.
recall.answer: Bedrock does not train its base models on your prompts or data, and your fine-tuned customizations stay private to your account.

sections.title: Decision trees: the whole exam on one page

keyTerms.definition: Same knowledge with better answers: rewrite the prompt.
New private or current facts: fetch them at query time.
Use a foundation model through an API instead of training your own.
The AWS service that builds chatbots.

recall.question: New private facts that change weekly: which customization does the tree pick?
recall.answer: RAG: fetch the facts at query time instead of baking them into weights.

keyTerms.definition: Serves foundation models you do not train, through one API.
Trains and hosts models you build from your own data.
Adds facts at query time; the weights never change.
Builds new behavior into the model's weights.

recall.question: What is the one-line difference between RAG and fine-tuning?
recall.answer: RAG adds facts at query time with weights unchanged; fine-tuning builds behavior into the weights.

sections.title: One look at the API (not on the exam)

keyTerms.definition: The Bedrock call: the request carries the model, the messages, and the settings.
The Python library for calling AWS services.

recall.question: What does a converse() request carry, and what comes back?
recall.answer: The request carries the model, the messages, and the settings; the response carries the generated text and the reason it stopped.

keyTerms.definition: Video lectures for the mental model, then docs, then practice questions, then revision.
A perfect AIF-C01 score; the scorer whose four-layer system this section follows.

recall.question: What study order did the 1000/1000 scorer use?
recall.answer: Video lectures first for the mental model, then docs, then practice questions, then revision.

keyTerms.definition: Labeled data predicting a category, like fraud versus legitimate.
Huge volumes scored on a schedule at the lowest cost per prediction.
RAG over your documents, with answers quoting and citing retrieved pages.
Foundation models that take actions through action groups calling your APIs.

recall.question: A 4,000-page manual changes weekly and answers must cite the page. Which approach fits?
recall.answer: RAG with Bedrock Knowledge Bases: fine-tuning goes stale within days and cannot cite pages.

recall.question: In phase 2 the assistant must file return tickets in the order system on its own. Which approach fits?
recall.answer: Bedrock Agents with action groups calling the order API: filing tickets means taking actions through tools.

recall.question: An auditor wants every Bedrock API call from last quarter, with caller and time. Which service fits?
recall.answer: CloudTrail: it logs every API call with caller identity and timestamp.
